reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A hereditary form of hypertension distinguished by hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) metabolic acidosis, essentially the mirror image of Gitelman syndrome
Caused by mutations in the WNK1 or WNK4 kinases, or in their regulators KLHL3 and CUL3, which increase activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal tubule
Kidney function is typically preserved, so the hyperkalaemia is not explained by renal failure
Enhanced distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands volume and reduces sodium delivery to the potassium- and acid-secreting segments, producing hyperkalaemia and acidosis
It is characteristically and often dramatically responsive to low-dose thiazide diuretics, which inhibit the overactive cotransporter
Consider it in a patient with hypertension, unexplained hyperkalaemia, normal GFR, and low or suppressed renin
Hypercalciuria may occur, in contrast to the hypocalciuria seen in Gitelman syndrome
Long-term control of blood pressure and potassium usually prevents complications
reference.pathophysiology: Gordon syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type II) arises from dysregulation of the WNK kinase signalling network that controls the distal convoluted tubule. Mutations in WNK1 or WNK4, or in the KLHL3-CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex that normally degrades WNK kinases, lead to excessive activity of the sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC). Increased salt reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule causes volume expansion and hypertension while diverting sodium away from the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron, thereby reducing the electrochemical drive for potassium and hydrogen secretion. The result is hyperkalaemia and hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with suppressed renin.
additionalDifferentials: Hypoaldosteronism (including type IV renal tubular acidosis)
Drug effects (e.g. RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics)
Primary aldosteronism (as a contrasting hypertension cause)
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate to document hyperkalaemic hyperchloraemic acidosis
Plasma renin and aldosterone (renin typically low)
Estimation of GFR to confirm preserved kidney function
Genetic testing for WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3 mutations
redFlags: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes or arrhythmia risk
Family history of early hypertension with electrolyte disturbance
reference.prognosis: The syndrome generally responds well to thiazide therapy with normalisation of blood pressure, potassium, and acid-base status, and the long-term outlook is favourable when treated.
pitfalls: Attributing the hyperkalaemia to renal failure despite a normal GFR
Missing the diagnosis because hypertension coexists with hyperkalaemia (an unusual combination)
Failing to appreciate the striking response to low-dose thiazides
Confusing it with type IV renal tubular acidosis without considering the genetic cause
